units.title: Recursion contracts, backtracking and sound pruning
outcomes: State the contract of a recursive enumeration: the state carried, the base case, and what each call hands back to its parent.
Implement choose, recurse, unchoose from a blank file with push-pop symmetry and snapshot-by-value, so every complete candidate is visited exactly once.
Add a sound prune and a duplicate-skip rule, with tests that fail when the bound cuts a valid candidate or the skip misses one.
units.why: Backtracking is the baseline every smarter search must beat. If the contract is vague, pruning looks like an optimization instead of what it is: a claim that the cut branches hold no solution.

next.note: Read the recursion-tree cost of your enumeration before calling it slow.
Repeated subproblems turn this chassis into memoized search later.

study.title: Backtracking, Chapter 2
study.locator: N Queens opening (printed pp. 71 to 73) and The General Pattern (printed pp. 79 to 80)

focus: The path is identical at entry and exit: every push has a matching pop in the same scope, and every snapshot copies the path instead of storing the live list.

The start-index chassis (subsets, combinations) and the used-mask chassis (permutations) take different duplicate-skip predicates. Sorting comes first in both, and the two predicates are not interchangeable.

A prune is a claim, not a speedup: the cut branch provably holds no solution, as with a negative remaining target over positive candidates or an attacked queen square. Bitmask state passed by value needs no undo step.
Output size sets the floor: subsets cost Theta(n times 2 to the n), permutations cost Theta(n times n factorial), and LC 46 stays small because n factorial explodes.
units.reproduce: From a blank file in Python 3.13.14, implement subsets and bitmask N-Queens. subsets([1, 2, 3]) returns 8 subsets; N-Queens counts are 2 for n equal to 4 and 92 for n equal to 8. Add a pytest file that checks every reported subset against the input set and every queen board for shared columns and diagonals.
traps: Appending the live path instead of a copy. Every snapshot aliases one list, later pushes mutate all of them, and the result finishes as copies of an empty path.
Skipping the unchoose half on one exit path, such as an early return that pops but forgets to clear used[i]. Keep push and pop adjacent in the same scope so no exit can split them.

An unproved prune that keeps sample tests green. Sort-then-skip on unsorted input misses valid candidates; CPython raises RecursionError at the default limit of 1000 frames (checked with sys.getrecursionlimit on 3.13.14), so raising the limit papers over a depth problem instead of bounding it.

selfTest.q: Why must the result store path.copy() rather than path?
selfTest.a: path keeps mutating after the snapshot. Storing the reference makes every entry reflect the final empty path instead of the candidate at snapshot time.

selfTest.q: What does the plain LC 78 algorithm emit on [1, 2, 2], and what is the fix?
selfTest.a: Eight subsets with a duplicated [2] and a duplicated [1, 2]. Sort first, then skip with i greater than start and nums[i] equal to nums[i-1], which keeps exactly one canonical index sequence per distinct multiset.

selfTest.q: Permutations run but return too few orderings. Which line is missing?
selfTest.a: The unchoose half: used[i] set back to False alongside path.pop(). Without it the invariant sum(used) equal to len(path) breaks and sibling branches never revisit the element.

selfTest.q: What makes a prune sound?
selfTest.a: A proof that no cut branch holds a solution, for example remaining target below zero with positive candidates, or a queen square under attack. Samples alone cannot show this.

units.title: Divide and conquer, recurrences and partition-based selection
outcomes: Solve T(n) equal to 2T(n/2) plus n, T(n) equal to T(n/2) plus n, and T(n) equal to T(n-1) plus 1 with recursion trees, stating depth, per-level cost and leaf count.
Explain why floors and ceilings change the answer by at most a constant factor, and when an unbalanced split breaks the tree bound.
Implement deterministic linear-time selection by median of medians and check it against a sorted oracle with pytest on small shuffled inputs.
State the quickselect recurrence and its quadratic worst case, and point to the partition unit for the invariant and to the randomized unit for the expected cost.
units.why: Divide and conquer sets the price of every recursive algorithm you will write. Selection shows the same recurrence idea deciding between linear and quadratic time.

next.note: Partition invariant, quickselect implementation, adversarial pivots, and heap versus quickselect versus full sort.

study.title: Recursion, Chapter 1
study.locator: Sections on Mergesort, Quicksort and recursion trees, then Section 1.8 Linear-Time Selection with Quickselect, Good pivots and Analysis (printed pp. 35 to 39)
study.depth: Skip Fast Multiplication and Exponentiation here. They return with dynamic programming and number theory.

study.title: Recursion patterns: linear, tree, and divide-and-conquer
study.locator: The three call-tree shapes and how to read the shape from the recursive case
study.depth: Use it as the shape vocabulary for the tree accounting in Erickson. Memoization detail belongs to the dynamic programming stage.

focus: Tree accounting has three numbers: depth, cost per level, and leaf count. T(n) equal to 2T(n/2) plus n with T(1) equal to 1 gives depth 10 and 11264 at n equal to 1024, checked with a five-line evaluator.
One-sided recursion is a path, not a tree: T(n) equal to T(n/2) plus n sums to Theta(n), while T(n) equal to T(n-1) plus 1 sums to Theta(n squared). Dropping the combine cost changes the answer.
Groups of five guarantee a pivot that discards a fixed fraction on both sides, giving T(n) below T(n/5) plus T(7n/10) plus O(n), which sums to linear because 1/5 plus 7/10 is below 1.
Fixed-pivot quickselect on sorted input recurses on n minus 1 each level and is quadratic. The randomness or the median of medians is doing the work, not the partition loop.
units.reproduce: Closed book, solve T(n) equal to 2T(n/2) plus n with T(1) equal to 1 by tree: depth 10, per-level cost 1024, total 11264 at n equal to 1024, confirmed with a short evaluator. Then in Python 3.13.14 run seeded quickselect (seed 123) on a shuffled range(1000): k equal to 499 returns 499 in 4347 comparisons, matching sorted.
traps: Reading T(n) equal to T(n/2) plus n as n log n. Halving with linear combine is a geometric series summing below 2n; the log appears only when both halves are solved.
Applying tree intuition to unbalanced splits without checking: T(n) equal to T(3n/4) plus T(n/4) plus n is still n log n, but T(n) equal to T(n-1) plus n is quadratic.
Quoting linear quickselect without naming the pivot policy. First-element pivot on sorted input is the quadratic case, and this unit proves the recurrence rather than the partition code.

selfTest.q: Solve T(n) equal to T(n/2) plus n with T(1) equal to 1.
selfTest.a: Theta(n). Level costs are n, n/2, n/4 and so on, summing below 2n. The recursion is a single path, so there is no leaf multiplicity.

selfTest.q: Give the quickselect worst case: input, pivot rule, and comparison count.
selfTest.a: Sorted input with first or last element as pivot. Partitions are 0 and n minus 1 at every level, so comparisons total n times n minus 1 over 2.

selfTest.q: Why is median-of-medians linear?
selfTest.a: Its recurrence is T(n) below T(n/5) plus T(7n/10) plus O(n). The subproblem fractions sum to 9/10, below 1, so the level costs form a convergent geometric series.

selfTest.q: What does this unit own that the partition unit does not, and vice versa?
selfTest.a: This unit owns recurrence analysis and deterministic median of medians. The partition unit owns the partition invariant, the quickselect implementation, adversarial pivots, and the top-k tradeoff.

units.title: Greedy choice, optimal substructure and exchange arguments
outcomes: State the greedy-choice property and optimal substructure of a new problem in one paragraph each, before writing any loop.
Prove a greedy rule with an exchange argument that preserves feasibility and never worsens the objective.
Prove a greedy rule with a staying-ahead invariant that compares the greedy prefix against every optimal prefix.
units.why: Greedy is the shortest path from idea to code and the easiest place to be confidently wrong. The proof is the algorithm, so write it before the loop.

next.note: Practice refuting plausible greedy rules, then prove earliest-finish scheduling.
Optimal substructure without a safe greedy choice forces dynamic programming.

study.title: Huffman encoding
study.locator: The algorithm; Watching it run on the worked frequencies; Why Huffman codes are optimal: the sibling exchange and the optimal-substructure recurrence

study.title: Greedy Algorithms, Chapter 4
study.locator: Section 4.1 Storing Files on Tape for the first exchange argument, Section 4.3 General Pattern for the exchange template and stays-ahead, Section 4.4 Huffman Codes (printed pp. 159 to 169)
study.depth: Skip Section 4.5 Stable Matching. It is not needed for the proof templates.

focus: Exchange has a fixed shape: take an optimal solution, swap its first differing choice for the greedy one, show validity kept and the objective not worse, then induct on the rest.
Staying-ahead has a different shape: the greedy frontier dominates every optimal prefix at each step, as with Jump Game max reach. Pick the template that matches the state you can compare.

Optimal substructure must hold after the greedy choice. In Huffman coding, merging the two least frequent symbols leaves a smaller instance whose optimum sits inside the full optimum through the weight recurrence.
Partition Labels is the stays-ahead drill: last occurrence table, extend the part end, cut at i equal to end, in O(n) time and O(1) extra space.
units.reproduce: From a blank file in Python 3.13.14, implement Partition Labels from its invariant and run it on ababcbacadefegdehijhklij to get [9, 7, 8]. Closed book, write the Huffman exchange step: swapping a least frequent symbol into a deepest sibling leaf changes total cost by at most zero.
traps: Proving by example. Passing samples shows the code runs; only the exchange or staying-ahead step shows no optimal solution beats it.
An exchange that breaks feasibility. Swapping must keep the prefix-free sibling structure in Huffman coding and disjointness in scheduling, or the transformed optimum is not a valid candidate.

Staying-ahead on the wrong measure, such as comparing part counts instead of frontier positions. Coins [1, 3, 4] with target 6 expose the habit: greedy takes 4 plus 1 plus 1 for 3 coins against optimal 3 plus 3.

selfTest.q: When do you reach for exchange, and when for staying-ahead?
selfTest.a: Exchange fits when any optimum can be rewritten choice by choice into greedy form. Staying-ahead fits when greedy maintains a frontier, such as reach or coverage, that dominates every optimal prefix at each step.

selfTest.q: State the Huffman exchange computation.
selfTest.a: Let x be a least frequent symbol and b a deepest leaf. Swapping their positions changes weighted path length by (freq[b] minus freq[x]) times (depth[x] minus depth[b]), which is at most zero since freq[b] is at least freq[x] and depth[x] is at most depth[b]. Repeat until the two least frequent symbols are deepest siblings.

selfTest.q: Why does total gas minus total cost at least zero guarantee a valid start?
selfTest.a: Start after the station where cumulative surplus hits its minimum. Every partial sum from there stays nonnegative, so the tank never empties over the full circuit.

selfTest.q: What optimal-substructure claim does Huffman coding need after the greedy merge?
selfTest.a: Merging the two least frequent symbols into one parent leaves a smaller coding instance, and an optimal tree for the smaller instance extends to an optimal tree for the original through the weight recurrence.

study.title: Interval scheduling: the comparator is the algorithm
study.locator: Why obvious finds the wrong answer; Why sort-by-end is optimal; Worked LC 435; strict less-than versus less-equal for LC 435 versus LC 56

study.title: Greedy thinking: the failure half
study.locator: Where greedy fails, with coins [1, 3, 4] and the decision rule
study.depth: Read only the failure section and the decision rule. The proof templates were covered in the previous unit.

study.title: Scheduling Classes, Section 4.2
study.locator: Section 4.2 (printed pp. 161 to 163): the earliest-finish rule and its exchange argument

focus: The comparator is the algorithm: sort by end time, keep an interval exactly when its start is at least the current end. Touching intervals are allowed in LC 435.
The exchange step replaces the optimal first interval with the earliest-finishing one: it ends no later, so the rest stays disjoint, and induction finishes the proof.
Sort-by-start fails on nesting: [[1, 100], [2, 3], [3, 4]] keeps the long interval and removes 2, while the optimum keeps the two short ones and removes 1.
LC 435 and LC 56 differ at the boundary: keep-touching uses strict less-than, merging uses less-equal with a max update. Pasting one boundary into the other is the standard bug.
units.reproduce: From a blank file in Python 3.13.14, implement earliest-finish: [[1, 2], [2, 3], [3, 4], [1, 3]] returns 1 removal. A pytest loop over 500 small instances from random.Random(7) agrees with the brute-force maximum on all 500 cases.
traps: Sorting by start or by duration. Both fail on nested intervals, and both pass friendly sorted samples, so the test family must include nesting.
Merging touching intervals in LC 435. [[1, 4], [4, 5]] removes nothing under LC 435 but merges under LC 56; the comparator is shared and the boundary is not.
Trusting sample tests for a greedy rule. Shrink each candidate rule against the others until the smallest input where they disagree, and check nested and touching cases first.

selfTest.q: Give the earliest-finish exchange step in one move.
selfTest.a: Let g1 be the earliest-finishing interval and o1 the first interval of an optimal set. o1 ends no earlier than g1, so replacing o1 with g1 keeps the set disjoint and no smaller; induct on the rest.

selfTest.q: Give the minimal counterexample to sort-by-start for maximum non-overlapping intervals.
selfTest.a: [[1, 100], [2, 3], [3, 4]]. Start order keeps [1, 100] and removes 2. The optimum keeps [2, 3] and [3, 4] and removes 1.

selfTest.q: What does [[1, 4], [4, 5]] give under LC 435 and under LC 56?
selfTest.a: LC 435 removes 0 because touching is allowed. LC 56 merges to [1, 5]. Same comparator, different boundary.

selfTest.q: How do you hunt a counterexample to a new greedy rule?
selfTest.a: Shrink to the smallest input where two candidate rules disagree, trying nested, touching, and equal-endpoint cases first. A rule that survives only sorted samples is not proved.

units.why: Random pivots turn a quadratic worst case into linear expected time. The guarantee only means something if you can say what is expected, over what randomness, and with what tail.

study.title: Expectation, linearity, and deviation bounds
study.locator: Session 32 (Chapter 18.4 to 18.5: expectation and linearity of expectation) and Session 33 (Chapter 19.1 to 19.3: Markov, Chebyshev, variance)

focus: Las Vegas means the answer is fixed and the time is random, as with quickselect, Fisher-Yates, reservoir, and rejection sampling. Monte Carlo means the answer itself may be wrong within a bounded error.
Linearity of expectation needs no independence, so indicator variables over pivot comparisons sum directly to the expected count.
This unit owns the expected-cost derivation for random pivots. Deterministic median of medians lives in the previous unit and partition code lives in the partition unit.
Expected cost is a mean; high-probability bounds tail risk through Markov, Chebyshev, or Chernoff. Treap depth is the worked example of the stronger claim.
units.reproduce: In Python 3.13.14, simulate rand10-from-rand7 rejection with seed 0 over 20000 trials: mean rand7 calls are 2.459 against theory 2 times 49 over 40 equal to 2.45. Run seeded quickselect (seed 123) on a shuffled range(1000) with k equal to 499: it returns 499 in 4347 comparisons. State sizes, seed, trials, and theory value with each run.
traps: Reading expected O(n) as fast on every run. The tail exists, so report trial counts and seeds, and never promise a single-run bound from an expectation.
Unseeded RNG inside tests. The suite passes until it does not; seed random.Random explicitly and record the seed with the expected output.
Modulo bias in hand-rolled reduction: mapping two rand7 calls mod 10 favors some digits because 49 outcomes do not split evenly, so rejection keeps 1 to 40 and redraws 41 to 49.

selfTest.q: Is quickselect Las Vegas or Monte Carlo, and what is random about it?
selfTest.a: Las Vegas. It always returns the correct kth element; only the number of comparisons varies with the random pivot choices.

selfTest.q: Why does linearity of expectation apply to quickselect comparison indicators?
selfTest.a: Expectation of a sum equals the sum of expectations with no independence requirement, so dependent comparison events still sum directly.

selfTest.q: What is the difference between expected treap depth and depth with high probability?
selfTest.a: Expected depth is a mean over random priorities. The high-probability bound says all but a tiny fraction of runs stay within O(log n), which needs a tail inequality rather than linearity alone.

selfTest.q: What must an empirical check of a randomized claim record?
selfTest.a: Input sizes, seed, trial count, theory value, and tolerance. For example: 20000 trials at seed 0 give 2.459 rand7 calls per rand10 against theory 2.45.

study.title: Sampling estimation
study.locator: Session 34 (Chapter 19.4 to 19.5): sample-mean polling and sample size choice

focus: Reservoir induction: with one slot, the old item survives with probability (i minus 1) over i, so each of the first i items is kept with 1 over i-1 times (i minus 1) over i equal to 1 over i.
Fisher-Yates has exactly n factorial equally likely paths. CPython random.Random.shuffle on 3.13.14 loops backwards with _randbelow, checked with inspect against the installed source.

Naive swap-with-any-index has n to the n paths over n factorial permutations and is biased; the rand-below-i variant (Sattolo) yields only single cycles; a 32-bit seed cannot reach all 52 factorial orders.

Empirical contract: sizes, seed, trials, tolerance. Over 4800 shuffles of 4 items the 24 permutation counts range from 178 to 223 against 200 expected, which is consistent with uniform and far from a starved or dominant permutation.
units.reproduce: In Python 3.13.14 with Hypothesis 6.169.0 and pytest 9.1.1, implement reservoir with k equal to 5: over range(100) with random.Random(0) it returns [63, 1, 2, 50, 34]. Over 4000 seeded trials on range(50), item 0 is kept with fraction 0.0985 against theory 0.1. A pytest file with a Hypothesis permutation-preservation property and the seeded uniformity loop passes with 2 passed.
traps: An off-by-one in the replacement range silently biases late items. The seeded fraction-kept check against 1 over i catches it; eyeballing a few samples does not.
Shuffling by sorting on random keys. Key ties and sort-order assumptions replace the n factorial path count with an implementation-defined distribution, so use Fisher-Yates.
Unseeded empirical tests that flake. Seed every RNG, record trials and tolerance, and rerun the exact command before claiming uniformity.

selfTest.q: Prove the reservoir induction step for one slot.
selfTest.a: Assume each of the first i minus 1 items is kept with 1 over i minus 1. Item i is kept with 1 over i, and each old item survives with (i minus 1) over i, giving 1 over i minus 1 times (i minus 1) over i equal to 1 over i.

selfTest.q: Why is swapping each position with any of n indices biased for n equal to 3?
selfTest.a: It has 3 to the 3 equal to 27 paths over 6 permutations, and 27 is not divisible by 6, so some permutations must get more paths than others.

selfTest.q: What does the Sattolo variant generate?
selfTest.a: Only single n-cycles: each position swaps with a strictly earlier index, so fixed points and short cycles never appear.

selfTest.q: What does the 178 to 223 range show about the shuffle?
selfTest.a: With 4800 shuffles over 24 permutations, 200 per permutation is expected. The observed spread is consistent with uniform noise; a biased shuffle would starve or flood some permutation far outside this band.
